unit.title: Perform basic welding using manual metal arc welding process (MMAW)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is a WPS used for?
options: To record the welder's hours and pay
To set out how the weld must be made
To list the welding machines the shop owns
To show the customer the price of the welds

questions.stem: Which electrode is usually the best choice for a structural joint in thick steel that must resist cracking?
options: E6013 rutile, for its smooth finish
E6010 cellulose, for its fast freezing
Any electrode, as long as the bead looks good
E7018 low-hydrogen, kept dry

questions.stem: A WPS gives a current range of 100–140 A for a 3.2 mm electrode. A trainee sets 160 A because 'it runs better'. What should you do?
options: Have him reset it within the range on the WPS
Allow it, as long as the finished weld looks good
Allow it, but tell him to weld faster
Lower it to 60 A to be safe

questions.stem: Why must a welder be qualified (tested) on a procedure before welding a job that calls for a qualified welder?
options: So the welder can charge a higher rate
So the job needs no inspection at all
To show the welder can make sound welds to it
So the welder can choose a different electrode

questions.stem: A WPS says 'preheat 100 °C minimum' for a thick joint. Which action is correct?
options: Skip it, as the Jamaican weather is already hot enough
Heat only the end where the weld starts
Heat it once, then weld for as long as needed
Heat the joint area and check it before welding

questions.stem: Why is a voltage reduction device (VRD) fitted to some MMAW machines?
options: To lower the voltage at the holder when not welding
To make the arc hotter and easier to strike
To save power, so that the electricity bill is lower
To stop the machine from overheating

questions.stem: Welding in a hot, humid workshop raises the risk of electric shock. Why?
options: Hot air carries current from the holder
The machine gives a higher voltage in the heat
Sweat makes skin and clothing conduct better
Humid air makes the arc jump to the welder

questions.stem: Welding fume is known to harm health over time. Which control should come first at a fixed welding bench?
options: A dust mask, worn only when the fume looks thick
Local extraction that captures fume at the arc
Opening a window at the far end of the shop
Welding faster so less fume is made

questions.stem: Why should welding on galvanised steel be avoided, or done only with extra controls?
options: Zinc makes the weld shine too brightly
Zinc stops the electrode from striking
Galvanised steel cannot be welded at all
Zinc fume can cause metal fume fever

questions.stem: A welder must weld inside a small steel tank. Which of these is essential?
options: A permit, ventilation and a standby person
Only a brighter lamp so the joint can be seen
Working alone, so no one else is put at risk
Using oxygen to keep the air fresh inside

questions.stem: Why must the return lead be clamped to the job itself, and not to a pipe or the steel frame of the building?
options: So the arc is brighter and easier to see
Stray current can heat or damage other parts
So that the cable is as long as possible
So the building is earthed through the welder

questions.stem: A trainee changes an electrode with a bare hand while the machine is switched on. What is the risk?
options: None, as the voltage is too low to be felt
The electrode will burn out more quickly
Shock, especially if the hand is damp
The holder will lose its grip on the rod

questions.stem: Why does an MMAW power source have a 'drooping' (constant current) output?
options: So the current rises sharply as the arc gets longer
So the voltage stays the same whatever the arc length
So the current stays steady as arc length varies
So the machine can also be used for MIG welding

questions.stem: What is one advantage of an inverter welding machine over an old transformer machine?
options: It is lighter and easier to move to the job
It never needs to be checked, tested or serviced
It can be used in the rain without risk
It gives no open-circuit voltage at all

questions.stem: On a site job, a long welding cable gets hot and the arc is weak. What is the likely cause?
options: The electrodes are far too small for the job
The machine is set to AC instead of DC
The work clamp is fixed much too close to the joint
The cable is too thin for its length and current

questions.stem: A machine is rated 250 A at 30% duty cycle. At 250 A, how many minutes must it rest in every 10 minutes?
options: 3 minutes
7 minutes
10 minutes
2.5 minutes

questions.stem: On a DC job, the arc keeps being pushed to one side near the end of the joint. Which change usually helps?
options: Change to AC, or move the work clamp
Use a longer arc and a faster speed
Increase the current as far as it goes
Use a larger electrode at the same current

questions.stem: Which polarity is normally used for E6010 cellulose electrodes?
options: AC only
DC electrode negative only
DC electrode positive
Any polarity at all

questions.stem: Why are low-hydrogen electrodes such as E7018 kept in a heated oven once the packet is opened?
options: To make them strike far more easily on cold plate
To keep the flux soft so it does not crack
To melt off any rust on the core wire
Damp flux adds hydrogen, which can crack welds

questions.stem: Which electrode type gives deep penetration and a fast-freezing pool, and is often used for root runs in pipe?
options: Rutile (E6013)
Cellulose (E6010)
Low-hydrogen iron powder (E7018)
Stainless steel (E308)

questions.stem: In the code E7018, what does the last digit, 8, tell you?
options: The electrode is 8 mm across its core wire
It has 8% iron powder in the flux
The flux type and the current it can use
It can be used in 8 positions

questions.stem: An electrode's flux is cracked and partly broken off near the end. What should be done?
options: Do not use it; it will not shield the arc properly
Use it, but turn the current up much higher than usual
Wet it to stick the flux back on
Use it for the root run only

questions.stem: Why is the electrode diameter chosen to suit the plate thickness and the weld position?
options: Bigger electrodes always give stronger welds
Too big a rod gives a pool too large to control
Small electrodes use much less power from the mains
The diameter sets the colour of the slag

questions.stem: Why must a stainless steel job be welded with a stainless steel electrode, and not a mild steel one?
options: Mild steel rods will not strike on stainless
Mild steel rods give too much spatter
Stainless rods are cheaper to buy
The weld would rust and could crack

questions.stem: Heat input (kJ/mm) = volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1 000). What is it for 24 V, 120 A and 150 mm/min?
options: About 1.15 kJ/mm
About 0.86 kJ/mm
About 11.5 kJ/mm
About 2.30 kJ/mm

questions.stem: A 300 mm weld run takes 2 minutes to complete. What is the travel speed?
options: 600 mm/min
300 mm/min
150 mm/min
100 mm/min

questions.stem: The throat of an equal-leg fillet weld is about 0.7 times its leg length. What is the throat of a fillet with 8 mm legs?
options: 8.0 mm
5.6 mm
4.0 mm

questions.stem: A job needs 4.5 kg of 3.2 mm electrodes. They come in 2 kg packets. How many packets must be ordered?
options: 2 packets
2.25 packets
4 packets
3 packets

questions.stem: A vertical joint usually needs a little less current than the same joint welded flat. If the flat setting is 120 A, which is a sensible vertical setting to try first?
options: About 150 A
About 120 A
About 105 A
About 60 A

questions.stem: When welding vertical up with a weave, why is the electrode paused briefly at each side of the joint?
options: To fill the edges and prevent undercut
To let the slag run down out of the pool
To cool the electrode so it lasts longer
To make the bead as high as possible

questions.stem: When a fillet weld is made in the horizontal position, how is the electrode usually aimed?
options: Straight down at the bottom plate only, at 90°
Straight at the upright plate only
Flat along the joint, pointing forward
Into the root, at about 45° between the plates

questions.stem: In a multi-run weld, why must each run be cleaned of slag before the next is laid?
options: So the next run is easier to see in the dark
Slag left in will be trapped as an inclusion
So the plate cools down faster between runs
So less electrode is needed for the next run

questions.stem: Why is a maximum interpass temperature sometimes given on a WPS?
options: Too much heat between runs can harm the steel
So that the welder can take a break between runs
To tell the welder when the slag can be removed
So that the plate never needs any preheat

questions.stem: When restarting a bead after changing the electrode, where should the new arc be struck?
options: On the plate beside the joint, then drag it in
Right at the start of the joint, over the old bead
Just ahead of the crater, then back into it
Anywhere, as long as the slag is not removed

questions.stem: A weld has lack of fusion along the side wall of the joint. Which is a likely cause?
options: Current much too high and travel much too slow
Current too low or the wrong electrode angle
The electrode was too dry
The plate was cleaned to bright metal

questions.stem: A root run has not penetrated through the joint. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Root gap much too wide and current far too high
The electrode was dried in an oven
Slag was removed between runs
Root gap too small or root face too large

questions.stem: Cracks appear in a thick steel joint some hours after it was welded with damp low-hydrogen electrodes and no preheat. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hydrogen cracking from damp rods and no preheat
Undercut caused by holding much too long an arc
Surface spatter caused by far too high a current
Porosity, from a short arc length

questions.stem: Porosity appears only at the start of each weld made with E7018 electrodes. What is a likely cause and cure?
options: Far too much current; turn it down by half
Rod too dry; dip it in water first
Long arc at the start; strike ahead, then back
Plate too clean; leave some rust on it

questions.stem: Undercut is found along the top toe of a horizontal fillet weld. Which change will most help?
options: Raise the current and travel faster
Use a longer arc to spread the heat
Point the electrode more at the upright plate
Lower the current and shorten the arc

questions.stem: A trainee's bead is rough and uneven with a lot of spatter. When you watch him, his arc length keeps changing. What should you coach first?
options: Raise the current as high as it will go
Keep a short, steady arc length
Weave much wider on every pass
Change to a larger electrode at once

questions.stem: Which test shows the inside of a fillet weld by breaking it open, for training or procedure checks?
options: A fillet break (fracture) test
A hardness test on the weld face
A visual check of the surface
A leak test with soapy water

questions.stem: What does a macro-etch test show?
options: The weld's tensile strength in MPa
Any hidden rust under the paint on the plate
Fusion and penetration on a cut and etched face
The welder's speed and the current used

questions.stem: A guided bend test is made on a butt weld test piece. What does it mainly check?
options: The weld's colour, ripple and surface finish
That it is sound and bends without cracking
The exact current used to make the weld
How fast the weld was made

questions.stem: You are supervising three trainees in the welding bay. Which check matters most before they strike an arc?
options: That each one has a different electrode type
That the machines are set to the highest current
That the bay door is shut to keep in the heat
PPE, screens, leads and the work area are safe

questions.stem: Why should a weld repair be written into the job's weld records?
options: So it can be inspected and traced later
So the welder can be paid twice for it
Repairs never need to be inspected
So the customer is charged for the welder's break

essays.stem: Explain what a WPS contains, and how a welder and a supervisor each use it on a job.
essays.modelAnswer: A WPS (welding procedure specification) is a written set of instructions that says exactly how a weld must be made so that it will be sound. It usually gives: the welding process (MMAW); the parent metal type and the thickness range; the joint design, with the bevel angle, root face and root gap; the welding position; the electrode type and diameter for each run; the current range, polarity and sometimes the voltage and travel speed; the preheat and interpass temperatures; the number and order of runs and the cleaning between runs; and any treatment after welding and the inspection needed. The welder reads the WPS before starting, sets up the joint and the machine to it, and stays inside its ranges. The supervisor checks that the welder is qualified for that WPS, that the right electrodes are issued, and that the settings, preheat and fit-up match it, and records the checks. If something on the job does not fit the WPS, the work stops and the supervisor or engineer decides what to do.
markingPoints: Says what a WPS is: written instructions for making a sound weld
Contents: process, metal and thickness, joint design, position
Contents: electrode, current, polarity, preheat and interpass, runs, inspection
Welder reads it, sets up to it and stays within its ranges
Supervisor checks qualification, electrodes, settings and fit-up, records, and stops work outside it

essays.stem: Compare E6013, E6010 and E7018 electrodes: their flux type, polarity, penetration, storage and typical jobs. Say which you would choose for a structural beam connection, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: E6013 is a rutile electrode. It runs on AC or DC, has a soft, smooth arc, medium to shallow penetration, easy slag removal and a neat finish. It must be kept dry but does not need an oven. It suits light fabrication such as gates and grills. E6010 is a cellulose electrode. It runs on DC electrode positive and has a forceful, digging arc with deep penetration, a fast-freezing pool and a lot of spatter. It is kept in its packet as the maker says and is not oven-dried like low-hydrogen rods, because its flux needs some moisture. It is used for root runs in pipe and on dirty or rusty work. E7018 is a low-hydrogen, iron-powder electrode. It runs on DC (some types also on AC), gives medium penetration and strong, tough, crack-resistant weld metal. Once opened it must be kept dry in a heated oven or quiver. It suits structural steel, thick sections and steels that may crack. For a structural beam connection I would choose E7018, because its weld metal is strong and tough and its low hydrogen reduces the risk of cracking in thick, restrained joints.
markingPoints: E6013: rutile, AC or DC, smooth arc, shallow to medium penetration, light work
E6010: cellulose, DCEP, deep penetration, fast-freezing, root runs
E7018: low-hydrogen iron powder, strong and tough, structural and thick work
Storage: E7018 in an oven or quiver; E6010 not oven-dried; E6013 kept dry
Chooses E7018 for the beam, with reasons (strength, toughness, low cracking risk)

essays.stem: You are setting up MMAW work on a building site in Montego Bay using an engine-driven welder. Explain the electrical, weather, fume and fire hazards, and how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Electrical: I check the machine before use, with the leads, holder and clamp in good condition and cables thick enough for their length. The work clamp goes on the job near the weld. I use a voltage reduction device if the machine has one, and keep gloves and clothing dry, because sweat in the heat makes a shock more likely. Weather: rain and wet ground raise the shock risk, so welding stops in rain unless the area is covered and dry, and the welder stands on a dry board or mat. Fumes: on site there is often a breeze, so I place the welder so that the fume blows away from the face, use portable extraction where possible, and a respirator where fume cannot be controlled, especially on painted or galvanised steel. The engine exhaust must not blow into work areas. Fire: I clear or cover anything that can burn, watch for dry grass and timber, keep an extinguisher at hand, get a hot work permit if the site needs one, and keep a fire watch after the work. I put up screens or barriers to protect other workers and the public from arc flash, and refuel the engine only when it is off and cool.
markingPoints: Electrical: checked leads and holder, cable size, clamp on the job, VRD, dry gloves and clothing
Weather: stop in rain unless covered; stand on a dry board or mat
Fume: position upwind, extraction or respirator, coatings, engine exhaust away from workers
Fire: combustibles cleared, extinguisher, permit if needed, fire watch
Screens or barriers for others; refuel only when the engine is off and cool

essays.stem: Explain how heat input is controlled in MMAW and why it matters. Then work out the heat input for 22 V, 110 A and a travel speed of 180 mm/min, using heat input = volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed × 1 000).
essays.modelAnswer: Heat input is the amount of arc energy put into each millimetre of weld. It depends on the voltage, the current and the travel speed: more current or voltage, or slower travel, gives more heat input. It matters because too much heat input gives a large, slow-cooling weld area with coarse grains, more distortion and sometimes lower toughness. Too little heat input gives fast cooling, which in thick or higher-carbon steel can cause hard zones and cracking, and can also cause lack of fusion. A WPS often gives a range. The welder controls heat input by keeping the current within the range, holding a steady arc length (which sets the voltage), keeping a steady travel speed, and using stringer beads or a narrow weave as the WPS says. Calculation: heat input = 22 × 110 × 60 ÷ (180 × 1 000) = 145 200 ÷ 180 000 = about 0.81 kJ/mm.
markingPoints: Defines heat input and the three things it depends on
Too much: coarse grain, distortion, lower toughness
Too little: fast cooling, hard zones, cracking, lack of fusion
Controlled by current, arc length, travel speed and bead type, within the WPS range
Correct answer: about 0.81 kJ/mm

essays.stem: A multi-run single-V butt weld in 12 mm plate is to be made in the flat position. Describe how you would prepare, tack, weld and clean the joint, run by run, to give a sound weld.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the WPS and the drawing. I bevel both plates to give the included angle the WPS gives (often about 60°), grind a root face of about 1.5–3 mm, and clean the bevels and about 25 mm each side to bright metal. I set the root gap with a spacer, line the plates up level, and tack at each end and in the middle, with a small pre-set against distortion. I clean the tacks and taper their ends, and check the fit-up before welding. The root run is made with a smaller electrode, often 2.5 mm, at the current the WPS gives, keeping the arc in the root to give an even penetration bead underneath. I clean the root fully, grinding off any high spots or slag lines. Then the hot pass and the fill runs are laid with 3.2 mm electrodes, removing all slag after every run and checking the interpass temperature. The cap is laid with a slight, even reinforcement that blends smoothly at the toes, with no undercut. I clean the finished weld, check it visually against the WPS, and record it.
markingPoints: Preparation: bevel to the WPS angle, root face, clean to bright metal
Fit-up: root gap with a spacer, alignment, tacks, pre-set, fit-up checked
Root run with a smaller electrode for even penetration, then cleaned and ground
Fill runs with full slag removal and interpass temperature checks
Cap with even reinforcement and no undercut; final inspection and record

essays.stem: Describe four weld defects: lack of fusion, slag inclusions, hydrogen cracking and porosity. For each, give the cause, how it would be found, and how it is prevented.
essays.modelAnswer: Lack of fusion is where weld metal has not melted into the side wall or the run below. It comes from too low a current, too fast travel or a wrong electrode angle. It is found by bend tests, fillet breaks or ultrasonic testing, and prevented by the right current, angle and speed. Slag inclusions are slag trapped in the weld. They come from poor cleaning between runs, deep valleys between runs, or too low a current. They are found by radiography or ultrasonic testing, or on a broken test piece, and prevented by cleaning every run fully and keeping a good bead shape. Hydrogen cracking happens in the weld or the heat-affected zone, often hours after welding. It comes from hydrogen from damp electrodes or dirty plate, a hard structure from fast cooling, and restraint. It is found by visual, magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing after a waiting time, and prevented by dry low-hydrogen electrodes, clean joints and preheat. Porosity is gas holes. It comes from damp electrodes, oil, paint or rust, a long arc or arc blow. It is found visually on the surface, or by radiography inside, and prevented by dry electrodes, clean metal and a short arc.
markingPoints: Lack of fusion: cause, how found and prevention
Slag inclusions: cause, how found and prevention
Hydrogen cracking: cause (hydrogen, hardness, restraint), how found (with a delay) and prevention
Porosity: cause, how found and prevention
Inspection methods matched sensibly to each defect

essays.stem: Explain the difference between destructive and non-destructive testing of welds. Describe two methods of each, and say when each kind is used.
essays.modelAnswer: Destructive testing cuts, bends or breaks a sample weld to see inside it and to measure how it behaves; the sample is destroyed, so it is used on test pieces for welder and procedure qualification, or on samples taken from production. One example is a bend test: a strip cut across the weld is bent round a former and must not crack open, which shows soundness and ductility. Another is a macro-etch test: a cut face is smoothed and etched so that the weld shape, fusion and penetration can be seen. A nick-break or fillet break test is another. Non-destructive testing checks the weld without damaging it, so it can be used on the actual job. One example is dye penetrant testing: a coloured liquid soaks into surface cracks and a developer draws it out to show them. Another is ultrasonic testing, where sound waves find defects inside the weld. Magnetic particle testing and radiography are others. NDT is used on finished work, often on the share of welds that the specification sets, and visual inspection always comes first, on every weld.
markingPoints: Destructive: the sample is destroyed; used for qualification and production samples
Two destructive tests (such as bend, macro-etch, nick-break) and what each shows
Non-destructive: no damage; used on the actual job
Two NDT methods (such as penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic, radiography) and what each shows
Visual inspection first, and NDT extent as the specification sets

essays.stem: Explain what arc blow is, why it happens, and the steps a welder can take to control it.
essays.modelAnswer: Arc blow is when the arc is pushed off its line, forwards, backwards or to the side, so the weld wanders and spatters and may have lack of fusion or porosity. It happens because the welding current makes a magnetic field around the electrode, the work and the cables. When the field is uneven, for example at the end of a joint, near a large mass of steel, in a corner, or because of where the work clamp is placed, it pushes the arc to one side. It is worst with DC and on magnetised steel, and rare with AC, because with AC the field keeps changing direction. To control it, the welder can change to AC if the electrode allows it; move the work clamp to another place or use two clamps; weld towards a heavy tack or away from the clamp; tilt the electrode against the direction of the blow; keep a short arc; lower the current; add more tacks, or use run-on and run-off tabs at the ends; and have magnetism removed from the steel if needed.
markingPoints: Defines arc blow and its effects on the weld
Cause: an uneven magnetic field (joint ends, steel mass, clamp position)
Worse with DC and magnetised steel; rare with AC
Remedies: AC, move the clamp, weld towards a heavy tack, tilt the electrode
Remedies: short arc, lower current, tacks or run-on and run-off tabs

essays.stem: As a supervisor, explain how you would control the storage and issue of electrodes in a welding shop, so that the right electrodes, in good condition, are used on each job.
essays.modelAnswer: I keep electrodes in a dry, locked store, in their packets, off the floor and labelled by type and size, using the oldest stock first. Low-hydrogen electrodes, once opened, are kept in a holding oven at the temperature the maker gives, and on the job they are carried in a heated quiver and returned at the end of the shift. Any that have been out too long or got damp are re-dried only as the maker allows, or scrapped. Cellulose electrodes are kept in their sealed packets and are not oven-dried. I issue electrodes against the WPS for each job, only in the amount needed, and record the type, size, batch number, the job and the welder. I make sure damaged, cracked or contaminated electrodes are thrown away and that stubs go in a metal bin. At the end of the shift, unused electrodes come back to the store or oven. I check and record the oven temperatures. This control makes sure the right electrode is used, prevents hydrogen cracking and porosity from damp flux, and lets a weld be traced to its electrode batch if a problem appears.
markingPoints: Dry, locked, labelled store; oldest stock used first
Low-hydrogen electrodes in an oven and quiver; re-dried only as the maker allows
Cellulose electrodes kept in their packets, not oven-dried
Issued against the WPS, with type, size, batch, job and welder recorded
Returns, damaged rods scrapped, oven temperatures recorded; explains traceability

essays.stem: A visual inspection finds undercut and a crack in a fillet weld on a steel stair stringer. Explain how you would report it, plan and make the repair, and check that the repair is acceptable.
essays.modelAnswer: First I mark the defects, photograph them and stop the stringer from being used. I write a non-conformance report giving the job, the weld, the defects (undercut and a crack), their size and position, and how they were found. I look for the likely cause: for the undercut, too high a current, too long an arc or a wrong angle; for the crack, perhaps damp electrodes, restraint or fast cooling. The repair is planned with the supervisor and written down. The crack is removed completely by grinding, and dye penetrant or magnetic particle testing confirms that it has gone before any welding. The groove is shaped so that it can be welded, cleaned to bright metal, and preheated if the WPS says so. The repair is welded to the WPS by a qualified welder using dry electrodes. The undercut is filled with a small run along the toe and blended in. After cooling, the repair is inspected visually and tested again by the same method, and the fillet size is checked with a gauge. The repair method, the results and the welder are recorded, and the report is closed when the repair passes.
markingPoints: Marks and photographs the defects, stops use, and raises a non-conformance report
Finds the likely cause of each defect
Removes the crack fully and proves it gone by NDT before welding
Repair welded to the WPS by a qualified welder; undercut filled and blended
Repair inspected and retested, results recorded, report closed

practical1.title: Multi-run fillet welds on tee joints to a written procedure, with inspection, a fillet break test and a weld record
practical1.brief: Your group will weld tee joints in 10 mm mild steel plate (two pieces about 150 mm × 75 mm for each joint), each with a three-run fillet weld of about 8 mm leg on one side, in the horizontal position, following a WPS. First, as a group, read the WPS the assessor gives (or complete one with the assessor): the electrode type and size, the current range, the polarity, the order of runs and the cleaning between them. One member leads the check of the welding bay before any arc is struck; another member leads the inspection. Every member fits, tacks and welds one tee joint while the assessor watches, and writes their current and run times on the weld record. When the joints are cool, each member measures another member's weld with a fillet gauge and records the leg sizes and any visible faults. Then the group chooses two joints, saws a short length from each, and breaks the fillet open in the press or vice (fillet break test), and looks at the broken face for lack of fusion, slag and porosity. Record the results and write a short report saying whether the procedure gave sound welds. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the WPS, weld record, report and photos once for the whole group.
materials: 10 mm mild steel plate, two pieces about 150 mm × 75 mm for each member
3.2 mm electrodes as the WPS gives (with an oven or quiver if they are low-hydrogen)
MMAW machines with screens and fume extraction
Chipping hammers, wire brushes and an angle grinder
Fillet weld gauge and a magnifier
Hacksaw or bandsaw, and a press or heavy vice for the break test
WPS, weld record sheet and report sheet
photos: The welding bay set up with screens and extraction, every member in PPE
The WPS and weld record filled in
A tee joint tacked and checked for square

practical2.title: Single-V butt weld in 10 mm plate to a procedure, with visual inspection, bend or nick-break tests and an inspection report
practical2.brief: Your group will weld single-V butt joints in 10 mm mild steel plate (two pieces about 200 mm × 100 mm for each joint) in the flat position, following the WPS the assessor gives: the bevel angle, root face and root gap, the electrodes for the root, fill and cap runs, and the current ranges. Plan the work as a group and share out the tasks. Every member prepares or checks the bevels, fits and tacks their own joint with the gap set by a spacer, and has the fit-up checked and recorded by another member before welding. Every member welds the root run with a 2.5 mm electrode, cleans it, then lays the fill and cap runs, cleaning between every run, while the assessor watches. When the joints are cool, inspect each one visually (the cap shape, undercut, and the root penetration underneath) and record the results. Then cut test strips across each weld as the assessor directs, and bend them in the Centre's bend test jig, or nick-break them if the Centre has no jig. Record what each test shows. Write an inspection report for the group: each joint, the results, any defects and their likely causes, and whether the WPS was followed. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: 10 mm mild steel plate, two pieces about 200 mm × 100 mm for each member, bevelled or ready to bevel
2.5 mm and 3.2 mm electrodes as the WPS gives
MMAW machines with screens and fume extraction
Angle grinder, files, root gap spacers and a weld gauge
Bandsaw or cutting machine for the test strips
Bend test jig or press (or a vice and hammer for nick-break tests)
WPS, fit-up record and inspection report sheet

Fitted and tacked own joint with the right root gap and alignment, and had it checked
Set the current within the WPS range for each electrode size
Made a root run with even penetration and cleaned it fully
Laid the fill and cap runs with full slag removal between runs
Own cap: even and slightly raised, with no undercut or surface porosity
Took part safely in cutting and testing the strips, and recorded the results accurately
Helped write the inspection report, naming faults and their likely causes
safety: Weld only in a booth or behind screens, with a helmet of the right shade, gloves and flame-resistant clothing
Keep gloves and clothing dry, and check the leads and holder before use
Use the extraction and keep your head out of the fumes
Wear a face shield over safety glasses for grinding and chipping; keep guards in place on the saw and the bend jig, and stand clear during testing
Treat all metal as hot; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
